messages:
evan: Heads up — after the continuous-batcher change deployed earlier this week, we see a sharp drop in prefix cache hit-rate for small interactive requests. 

michael: How sharp? numbers?

evan: From ~78% -> ~58% on the small-seq cohort (<=64 tokens). P99 latency for those requests moved from ~63ms to ~112ms. Throughput mostly stable.

sara: oof. did the batcher change kernel selection too or only queueing?

evan: queueing heuristics + changed mixing policy (we now mix across session affinity more aggressively to fill GPUs). Kernel selection path stayed the same but kernel prefetch patterns look different in traces.

dina: quick hypothesis: batch composition mixes prefixes from different users -> local KV prefix cache dominated by a few hot prefixes gets evicted more often. mixing increases cache churn.

eyan: ^exactly. flamegraph shows much higher time in kv-cache-miss handling and AGGREGATE_PREFIX_LOOKUP.

ryan: can you paste the perf trace?

evan: putting snippets below (from the perf-run):

```
[trace] request_id=abc123 seq=42 prefix_hash=0x7f3a key_miss=true 
  batch_size=18 batch_mix=[p1,p2,p7,p1,p3,p8,p1,...] 
  kv_fetch_time=12.4ms kernel_time=18.0ms
[trace] request_id=def456 seq=12 prefix_hash=0x2b1c key_miss=false 
  batch_size=18 batch_mix=[p2,p7,p1,p3,p8,p1,...] 
  kv_fetch_time=0.8ms kernel_time=22.1ms
```

michael: interesting — when same prefix appears multiple times in batch it's fine, but interleaving causes eviction and repeated remote fetches. do we know eviction policy? LRU with per-GPU slab?

evan: LRU-ish with per-GPU segments and an approximate counting window. It wasn't tuned for high interleaving. When mixing gets high, small hot prefixes no longer dominate the cache.

sara: any correlation with sequence length distribution? like long sequences holding KV entries in cache longer and pushing others out?
evan: yes — long seq requests pin larger KV spans and reduce effective cache capacity for short sequences. Combined with cross-session mixing it's worse.

dina: possible mitigations:
- keep affinity-windowing so we group same-prefix requests for short time slices
- add a tiny LRU-protected hot-prefix lane (static small hot set per-GPU)
- prefetch predicted next-prefixes for sessions with high locality
- change cache keying: include model_version+prefix_hash and a short per-session tag so duplicates align

ryan: i like affinity-windowing + hot-prefix lane. can we do it without blowing up latency SLO on cold-starts?

evan: we ran a sim: affinity-windowing with 50ms grouping reduced miss-rate back up to ~73% and P99 for small sequences dropped to ~78ms. Cold-starts increased by ~3-5ms on average due to waiting to group, but overall user-visible latency improved.

sara: what about dynamic thresholding — only enable grouping when queue occupancy below X so we don't slow down under high load?

evan: already prototyped that — thresholding helps. Under 70% GPU utilization we group for up to 40ms; above that we fall back to greedy dispatch. That preserves throughput.

michael: kernel selection note: if kv-fetch time spikes, some kernels that were optimal become memory-bound — we should prioritize kernels that do less mem-copy on miss path. open to adding a perf-driven kernel preference when miss-rate > Y.

evan: agreed. kernel pref selection can be driven by a simple rule: if observed kv-miss latency per batch > 5ms, prefer kernel path B (lower mem-copy but slightly slower compute). In our tests that knocked 5-10ms off overall P99 for missed batches.

dina: we should also log a compact tag in traces for "batch_mix_entropy" so we can correlate mixiness with misses automatically.

evan: added a PR to add batch_mix_entropy to logs (link: https://redwood.internal/p/1234) — infra-bot, can you kick an experiment on staging with grouping-on-low-load and kernel-rule enabled?

infra-bot: experiment job queued: staging/continuous-batcher/affinity-windowing-kernel-rule. Estimated runtime: 4 hours. Notifying eng-runtime when complete. :robot_face:

ryan: once we have staging results let's A/B test hot-prefix lane vs affinity-windowing. Also add per-prefix telemetry so we can see which prefixes benefit most.

sara: one more thought — we may be able to reduce kv-key churn by normalizing prefixes (strip session-specific salts) earlier in the pipeline. Might need product approval for that for some customers, but for internal workloads could help.

evan: noted. I'll run the staging experiment and collect hit-rate, batch_mix_entropy, p99, and per-prefix eviction rates. Posting an interim writeup after results. Thanks everyone :thumbsup:
